text.p: One day after debating Republican Bob Dole, President Bill Clinton on Monday stole support from one of Dole's key constituences, accepting the endorsement of more than 2,500 businesspeople.

Top executives from some of the nation's largest companies including Xerox Corp, Sprint Corp. and United Technologies Corp turned out to praise Clinton the morning after the debate, saying his administration had been good for big business.

The endorsement was unusual in U.S. politics, where industry has typically sided with Republicans rather than Democrats. But many of the executives including Sprint's William Esrey have appeared with the president in the past and their support for Clinton has long been known.

"I have wondered through the years why the Democratic Party should not have at least as much or more support from American business as the other party," Clinton told about five hundred business people at a speech in Stamford, Connecticut.
"We never thought that ... helping ordinary people live up to their full potential was inconsistent with trying to build a strong business environment," he added.

Appearing on the same stage, Esrey acknowledged how unusual was the show of support, saying there was a "growing, although sometimes reluctant, realization by corporate America that Democrat Bill Clinton has been good for American business."
The Clinton/Gore campaign announced that more than 2,500 chief executives and business leaders had endorsed the president, suggesting that this vindicated his management of the economy.
While accepting their endorsement, Clinton asked the businesspeople for more, saying he needed their help to make the recently enacted welfare reform law work.

"Only the private sector in America can prove that I was right to sign that bill, and those who thought I was wrong were wrong," he said. "The government cannot hire all these people ... This has basically got to be a private sector show."
Clinton made no direct reference to Sunday night's debate in Hartford, although White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters he was "absolutely delighted" with the outcome.

The president was scheduled to campaign later in the day in Manchester, New Hampshire, a state that is traditionally a Republican stronghold, and Portland, Maine, before returning to Washington early on Tuesday.
